title: The simple answer to improving productivity: asking employees
author: Bruce Daisley
summary: Bruce Daisley argues that the productivity and engagement problems of modern workplaces trace back to a loss of worker agency. He cites the Skills and Employment Survey, in which only a third of UK workers say they have discretion over how they do their jobs, down from two-thirds three decades ago. Interviewing the survey's co-lead Alan Felstead, he reports that more task discretion goes with higher productivity and better wellbeing, and that frontline workers are eager to say how their roles could improve when asked. The obstacle is that head offices often do not want that input and impose plans that feel wrong to those doing the work. Daisley connects this to Martin Seligman's new book on agency and to Octopus Energy's autonomy-first culture, and ends with Felstead's simple management advice to give employees voice and listen to them more.
points: The falling share of workers with discretion over their tasks is presented as a root cause of low engagement and low productivity, not a side effect.
Felstead's research finding is that the more task discretion people have, the more productive they are, and that small, job-specific choices lift autonomy most.
Frontline workers readily offer improvements when asked, so the gap is organisations unwilling to listen rather than employees unwilling to contribute.
Octopus Energy is offered as a working example of a culture defined mainly by giving everyone autonomy in their roles.
The practical leadership takeaway is to give employees greater voice and listen to them more before imposing a top-down plan.
